Baghdad History for Sleep 🌙 The Night Paper Changed the World

Watch on YouTube Listen on YouTube Music

Baghdad history for sleep: a calm night in 9th-century Baghdad, when paper was still fairly new in the city, with a translator, reed pens, ink and a Greek book.

Paper is the quiet star of this night. Baghdad, the Tigris, the paper and the caliph's library are real, and so are the scholars named in the old catalogues. Dawud, Nafi, Harith, Layla and Ibrahim are imagined, but people like them lived and worked here. Historians still discuss what the House of Wisdom was; where sources disagree, the narration says so.

What about a Board of Dust: The Banu Musa and a Sum on a Dust-Board?

We sit with Dawud and Nafi in a hired room in Baghdad, past the middle of this night in the eight hundred and fifties. Harith’s note waits. The folded sheet lies under a wooden weight, kept flat until the sum is done. Dawud draws a shallow tray across the boards and sets it level before his hands. The tray is for a sum he will try before Nafi starts the fair copy. The tray holds a thin bed of pale powder, and a fingertip draws only the figures that must wait.

What about the Stationers' Row: Paper Sellers and Booksellers of Baghdad?

We step out with Layla on the west bank in Baghdad, the night past its middle and the air gone cool. Keys knock softly. She has come for sheets, so Nafi will have a fresh bundle when the copying starts again at the table. Our feet find the packed earth, and a damp breath rises from the canal between the dark houses. She walks a little ahead in a woollen cloak, a folded cloth bag under one arm. In about eight hundred and ninety-one a geographer named al-Ya'qubi will set down what stands along this way.

What about Cakes of Ink: How Ink Was Made?

Past the middle hours we sit in the hired workroom with Dawud the translator and Nafi the copyist, and a dry round of black waits for the next sitting. Dawud sets a smooth stone beside it and breaks a corner free with his thumb. While he grinds, a little water darkens the powder as the pestle turns in slow circles. The black gathers into a paste he can thin whenever the well beside the reed needs filling again. Nafi slides the older book toward the far edge so the wet paste cannot touch a finished line.

What about a Reader and a Finished Page: A Medical Book in Arabic?

We are with Ibrahim in a courtyard house in Baghdad, on a quiet night in the middle of the ninth century. He sits with a finished copy on a low wooden stand, the reader who has waited for this book. He leans closer. A cool breath crosses the shaded opening and lifts the hem of his sleeve. His thumb keeps the outer edge of the page from curling up as he reads. The copy is a medical book, written in a fair hand and left to dry through the hours of copying.

What about the River before Morning: The Tigris at Dawn?

We come with Layla and Ibrahim to the river bank in Baghdad, in these middle years of the ninth century, as first light spreads thin and pale. The lane is empty. Our steps stay unhurried, and a cool edge meets us that was not in the room above the lane. Mist softens the far bank, and the broad flow keeps a low, even sound. A round boat rests in the shallows, close against the mud. It sits low. Its frame is built of pomegranate branches, and date-palm fronds are woven all round that frame until the sides make a circle.

0:00:00Intro · 242 words

It is a night in Baghdad, more than eleven hundred years ago. A lamp burns low over a Greek book and a fresh sheet of paper, and someone is turning one language into another, one careful line at a time.

This is Dreaming Ages. Over the next two hours, we'll sit with a copyist by a low lamp, cross a street of shuttered shops, and rest while the river keeps its sound. Nothing loud, nothing sudden, and nothing frightening. Just a slow voice, the sound of the river in the dark, and a street of shuttered shops.

Pull up the blanket, rest your head on the pillow, and I'll blow out the candle. Now, follow me back in time.

It's the middle of the eight hundred and fifties, a quiet night in Baghdad, on the west bank of the Tigris. A man we call Dawud has hired a small workroom for the late hours. He is a translator. On the table a Greek book lies open, and beside it a sheet of paper, brown, stiff, and a little polished. He works slowly, turning the book into Arabic, one line and then the next. The shutters are already closed. The lamp is lit. We step inside.

Baghdad, the Tigris, the paper, and the caliph's library are real, and so are the scholars named in the old catalogues. Dawud, Nafi, Harith, Layla and Ibrahim are imagined, but people like them lived and worked here.

0:03:06A Lamp over a Fresh Sheet: A Translator's Workroom in Baghdad · 1,383 words

We are with five imagined people in a hired workroom on the west bank, on a quiet night in the eight hundred and fifties. A low table holds an open Greek book and a fresh sheet, and two men sit so close their sleeves nearly touch. The room is warm. That warmth sits over the page, and the air between the two men stays almost still while they work.

I've made a free printable bedtime companion for tonight's story. It tells you a little more about the people and places you'll meet. And if you comment… goodnight… below, my reply has the link. Now, back to the hired workroom.

The man with the pen is Dawud, and the older Greek book lies open under his left hand. Translation is his work. He reads a short passage through, grasps what it means, and writes that sense in Arabic instead of matching every word. His right hand stays above the sheet until the next phrase is clear enough to set down.

Beside him sits Nafi, who will make the fair copy once a finished passage is set aside. He watches the hand. A clean sheet waits under a folded cloth, ready to lay over wet lines when they need to rest. The fair copy begins only when one line is left clear and the black has dried on the page.

Layla keeps the sheets, and she is the bookseller who has brought paper for the night's copying. She checks edges. Her thumb turns each sheet before one moves toward the table, and a small stack goes onto a low chest by the wall. Pale powder lies on an old binding in her lap, and she brushes it away with the side of her hand.

Ibrahim sits on a cushion near the chest, a young reader who has come to wait for a finished page. His hands rest quietly. He listens to the scratch of the pen, and his eyes stay on the lines as they appear one after another. When a sentence is done he leans a little, as if the new words might already be his to keep.

Near the door, which stands a little open to the lane, a man named Harith waits with a folded note. Dust marks his hem. He holds the note against his chest and does not step farther in until someone looks up from the work. A faint coolness comes in around his shoulder and fades before it can reach the open book.

Dawud's pen is a dried reed, pale brown along the shaft, with a dark tip where ink has stained the point. It is hollow. He turns it once between his fingers and holds the middle, and the shaft barely bends because the reed has gone hard. The cut end is narrow, and a thin dark film clings there until he sets the point down on the page.

To the right of the Greek book sits a small round pot of dark ink, its mouth wide enough for the reed. Wool soaks in it. The reed will take ink from that wet wool rather than from a deep pool, so the stroke can stay even. A short stick lies across the rim, darkened at one end, ready for when the black needs a stir.

He dips, and the first stroke comes out strong and dark, with clean edges along the fresh sheet. The reed is full. It writes several words before the black thins, and he watches that line rather than the Greek behind his wrist. When the stroke turns speckled he stops and lifts the reed, so no weak word is left standing in the text.

The sheet under his hand is pale, a little rough along one edge, and it holds each stroke where the reed has passed. The edge frays. Where the reed presses, the black sits in the surface, and he can see each letter while it is still wet. He draws his sleeve back from that wet band so the cloth will not smear the line just formed.

Nafi's own reed lies on the folded cloth, shorter than Dawud's and still clean along the tip. It has not written. He keeps a spare slip of reed in a fold of his belt, in case a point fails before the fair copy is done. When the translator nods, that clean pen will carry the finished sense onto the sheet Layla has set ready.

The Greek book is thick, and its cover has gone soft at the corners from many hands before this night. A thread hangs loose. The pages inside are crowded with small letters, and some lines have a faint mark where an earlier reader paused. Dawud keeps the book flat with his left palm so the page will not lift while he writes.

Beyond the wall the Tigris moves, and we hear it only as a far sound, low and steady under the night. The air is mild. The river stays a presence past the lane, while the faces at the table stay bent over the lines that are forming. Somewhere a cart wheel ticks once on stone, and then the street goes quiet around the hired room.

About a hundred years earlier, Abu Ja'far al-Mansur laid out this city as his capital on the west bank of the river. He founded it. In seven hundred and sixty-two he set down the round City of Peace, Madinat al-Salam, and that name still hangs over the lanes. The work on this table is a quieter kind of making than the laying of those first walls.

That round city had a double wall, and four gates set at equal distances around the circle. Roads ran inward. Four roads led toward the palace and the great mosque in the centre, each one keeping its own direction through the day. People came and went by those gates, passing between the circle and the land that lay outside the walls.

Dawud's sleeve has a small dark spot near the cuff, where the reed has brushed him on an earlier line. He notices it. Two fingers push the cloth back, and he returns to a phrase that will not settle, sounding it once under his breath. The letters he has already set stay dark and even, and he leaves them while he works on the stubborn phrase.

Layla counts the unused sheets in a low voice, touching only the corners so the faces stay clean. The stack is modest. She sets the next sheet where Nafi can find it, smoother side up, and then folds her hands into her sleeves. The old binding stays in her lap, and she waits with the paper ready beside the low chest.

A clay cup of water sits by Ibrahim's knee, and he drinks once without taking his eyes off the new line. The cup is plain. He sets it down on the mat and rests his hands on his knees again, in the dimmer part of the room. His place is the cushion, and he does not reach for the sheet until someone offers it to him.

Outside the door the lane is packed earth, pale where a little light from the room falls across the threshold. A shutter is shut. Farther along, a shop front is closed for the night, its boards fitted tight, and no voice comes from behind them. Harith's sandals are dusty from that lane, and he shifts his weight so the boards under him do not creak.

Dawud lifts his head, and Harith takes that look as leave to be heard at last. His voice is low. He says a wealthy man has sent him to ask for a medical book made plain in Arabic, for a household to use. Dawud hears him through, the reed still raised, and does not break in before the messenger has finished.

Harith steps in over the threshold and sets the folded note on the chest, clear of the fresh sheet. His thumbprint shows. Nafi shifts the clean copy a little to make room, and Layla's hand leaves the old binding so the note can lie flat. Dawud turns back to the Greek, finds the stalled phrase, and lowers the reed to finish the line he had begun.

0:12:51Paper that Takes the Pen: Brown Paper and Soot Ink · 1,575 words

We stay in the hired workroom as the night moves further on, and the Tigris is only a far sound beyond the wall. Nafi reaches across for a fresh piece of paper from the stack at his elbow. He lifts it. He turns the sheet toward the low light, while the room still holds the warmth of the afternoon and the Greek book lies open on the medical passage.

He runs a thumb along each face and finds both sides polished, a deep brown, opaque and stiff. The sheet has a medium thickness. It does not bend easily between his fingers as he holds it up. A book on paper of this kind, dated to the last months of eight hundred and sixty-six, is the oldest Arabic book on paper that survives.

Nafi holds the sheet beside his forearm to judge the breadth, and it matches the small size of a page a clerk might copy on. The corners are square and clean. The larger piece it came from was about twice that, formed in a mould a maker could hold in his hands. Dawud watches the edges and waits, because paper of this kind must not be rushed under the pen.

People call this paper waraq, a word that means leaves, and a warraq is the person who sells it. He may also make it. He may copy books on it for buyers who come to his shop, and Nafi works in that same line. The person who supplied this stack lives by the same name, and the word covers the maker, the merchant, and the hand that writes a fair copy.

An older word for paper is kaghad, and it came through Sogdian and through Uighur, tongues of the roads that run toward the east. It travelled far. The root is the Chinese name for paper made of mulberry bark, while the leaf on this table was made much closer to hand from rags and other waste fibres. Cloth is cut and beaten until the pulp can be lifted in a mould a man can hold.

The water drains away, and a wet leaf is pressed and left to dry. That plain making turns old cloth into a page. The page can carry a medical book through a long night of copying, as Dawud waits with the Greek lines open beside him. Nafi sets the brown sheet flat so the face stays clear until the reed is ready.

Another word, qirtas, sat in Arabic before waraq became the usual name, and it meant papyrus or parchment. It comes from the Greek chartes, a word for a leaf meant to take writing. Dawud hears that kinship. He looks from the Greek lines to the Arabic page under his hand, and his copy will sit on beaten rag fibre, not on a skin prepared as parchment.

Muslims met paper in Central Asia in the eighth century, long before this stack was cut, and Samarkand grew famous for sheets of that kind. A writer of a later century, al-Tha'alibi, said the paper of that city was more supple and more easily handled than papyrus. He also called it more convenient for writing than parchment. Nafi does not need the comparison, because the leaf in his hands already takes a thumb without cracking.

The face has been prepared so the ink will sit rather than sink straight through. Before a dried sheet can take a pen, it is sized with starch, and rice starch will serve as well as wheat. A later guide gives equal parts of chalk and starch. That mix belongs to a later century and is not what Nafi is checking now, as he feels the coat with his thumb.

After the size dries, a worker burnishes the paper with a smooth stone, or with glass, or with a shell. The strokes are long. They run until both faces feel firm and carry a dull polish that a thumb can find without looking. Nafi’s leaf has that finish already, and he tilts it toward the low light to see that the coat is even from edge to edge.

He sets the sheet down so the polished face waits for the reed. Dawud’s ink is the carbon kind, called midad, made from soot rather than from galls. A second family stands beside it in the craft. Iron-gall ink, called hibr, comes from oak-galls and an iron salt, and some makers blend the two so the black has both bodies.

Only soot ink is open on the table tonight. It sits dark in the well where the wool holds it, with a small stick beside the well to keep the mixture from settling. To make midad, the soot is ground fine and the greasy part is taken out. Gum-arabic water is added a little at a time until the black stays in the water and on the page.

Treatises of the tenth and eleventh centuries write that method down, though the way itself is older. For the other ink, gallnuts are boiled in water and the liquid is strained clear. Then gum arabic goes in. Green vitriol follows, and green vitriol is an iron salt that meets the gall as the mixture darkens in the pot.

Recipes of this kind are written in the tenth century and later, so no one can say just when this ink became common here. Because iron-gall ink bites into the fibres, a written word is very hard to take off. Officials trusted a mark that soaked in and stayed. That quality made paper safer for records than papyrus or a skin that could be cleaned and used again.

On papyrus, wet ink could be wiped or washed away before it set. A dried face could be rubbed back with a stone until the writing lifted. Paper drinks the black in. Nafi keeps a spare leaf near his knee, ready if a word goes wrong and must be begun again on a clean face.

Parchment could be cleaned and written on again, and the reused leaf is called a palimpsest, which Arabic calls tirs. al-Razi gives recipes for lifting ink from parchment, from papyrus, and from paper as well. His treatise comes from the next generation. Dawud keeps his eye on the soot in the well, because that is the black he will set down tonight.

Harun al-Rashid became caliph on 14 September, in seven hundred and eighty-six. Paper followed soon. By his reign workshops were at work in Baghdad, about seven hundred and ninety-four or ninety-five, and Ibn Khaldun credits the vizier al-Fadl ibn Yahya. Officials kept their records on it, because a line that had soaked in was hard for a later hand to scrape out.

Dawud writes as if each word of the medical passage must remain where the reed sets it down. In Harun’s reign al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf ibn Matar made the first Arabic Euclid, finished before about eight hundred and five. He set out points, lines, and proofs for readers who did not use Greek. He worked for Harun, and the habit of carrying a whole Greek book across into Arabic was already old by this night.

Dawud’s page tonight is a medical one, yet that same habit sits behind the lines he reads. al-Hajjaj later returned to the Elements and revised what he had written. About eight hundred and thirty-three he made a second Arabic version for al-Ma’mun. That caliph ruled from eight hundred and thirteen until eight hundred and thirty-three, and Arabic geometry then had two versions from the same translator.

Nafi smooths the leaf with the side of his palm, working from the centre out toward each edge, and the polish whispers under his skin. A few fibres lift. They settle back on the brown face, and Dawud shifts the Greek book a finger’s width so the line he needs sits where he can read it without leaning in. If a soot stroke sits a little soft at the edge, a scrap will show it before a fair line begins.

Nafi tears a narrow strip from a spoiled leaf and lays it at Dawud’s right hand for that first test. A fingertip finds a slight tooth under the polish, just enough for a reed to catch so a line does not skate. The starch holds the black in a clean track. Beside the Greek book stands a low stack of the same brown paper, each piece cut to one size.

Nafi counts them, and there are enough pieces for the chapter Dawud hopes to finish, with a few extra in case a line must begin again. A folded cloth lies at the corner, plain and soft from washing. He dries his hand on it so no damp print can sink into the sized surface. He waits until the page can lie flat under Dawud’s wrist without a mark from his palm.

He lets one corner droop, then brings it level, and the edge gives a soft tick against the wood. The paper has weight. That body comes from fibres beaten close, and it keeps a long line from wrinkling under the heel of a hand that rests too long. Nafi draws the sheet toward him until the near edge lies square with the table, and Dawud shifts the inkwell a little aside.

Nafi’s palm comes down and rests on the stiff brown sheet, holding the page steady while Dawud reaches for the reed.

0:23:59One Careful Line: Translating Greek into Arabic · 1,576 words

We stay with Dawud and Nafi in a hired workroom in Baghdad, deep in a night of the eight hundred and fifties. The feel is right. Dawud lifts a dried stalk from a bowl of water and turns it once between thumb and finger. Nafi sits with folded hands and watches each movement of the stalk. A line still has to be written, so the tool must be finished before any word goes down.

Scribal manuals, most of them from later years, recommend that a reed rest in water until the stalk takes on the right give. This one has had that rest. Nafi slides the bowl a little aside so the drip will not reach the page. Dawud lays the wet stalk on a folded cloth and reaches for the blade he keeps wrapped when it is not in the hand.

Dawud sets the stalk across his palm and measures a length that will sit well between the fingers. The blade is keen. One clean stroke takes off the spare end, and a few damp fibres cling to the edge of the knife. He holds the cut end up so Nafi can see the light ring where the hollow runs.

He pares the sides next, taking thin curls away so the point can be freed from the thicker body. Each curl drops onto the cloth. They lie there pale and slightly damp, stuck a little to the weave. Dawud turns the stalk and pares the other side, leaving a taper that will hold ink without spreading too wide.

The slant comes last, cut on a small wooden board called a miqatt, so the knife meets wood and not the bare table. He lays the taper flat. The blade travels across the tip at an angle, and the shaving comes away thin as a nail paring. Each script wants its own angle and its own thickness of tip, and this cut is meant for a steady book hand.

Plain wood is enough for a board like this, though later accounts speak of ivory or bone. A plain board dulls nothing. It keeps the knife from wearing on stone, and it gives the stalk a firm rest while the slant is made. Nafi brushes a curl off the near corner and sets it with the others along the folded cloth.

Inside the reed there is a soft pith, and that has to come away before the tip will behave. He shaves it out with the same blade, working along the hollow until only the hard outer shell remains. The shell carries the line. A pen left full of pith would blot, and the letters would thicken where they ought to stay fine.

After the slant, he splits the tip in two, following the grain of the stalk. The slit is short. It lets the ink run down to the page, and a pen without that split writes dry and skips. He tests the split with a thumbnail, then wipes the tip on the cloth so no loose fibre will catch in the first stroke.

A late guide sets a thickness between the index finger and the little finger, only an average, not a rule. Dawud holds his own fingers beside the finished tip. He nods once. The cut tip is neither heavy nor hair-fine, and it looks suited to hours of close writing on a page that must stay clear.

Dawud rolls his wrist and loosens the fingers that held the stalk through the cutting. Nafi straightens the cloth. He gathers the pale curls into a little heap at the far edge, away from the open book. The new pen waits beside that book, where the last copied line stopped and the next one has still to be made.

Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a Christian from al-Hira, was born in eight hundred and nine, and he came to know Syriac, Arabic, and Greek for this labour. Greek came later. He learned it after a quarrel with his teacher, and the quarrel sent him deeper into that older language. In time he returned, and the books he needed were sought, compared, and written out again over many years.

It is told that Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a leading physician of the city, lost patience with young Hunayn's questions and sent him away. The tale comes late. After that quarrel he learned Greek more deeply, and the two are said to have worked together once he had returned. The books went on between teacher and pupil after that early sharpness had passed.

His method, as he himself set it down, was to gather as many source copies of a book as he could find. He set them side by side. Comparing them fixed the text before a single sentence was turned, and a gap in one copy could be filled from another. Only then did writing into a new language begin, once the missing place had been supplied from a fuller manuscript.

Greek usually went into Syriac first in his hands, and only then from Syriac into Arabic. A student took that step. Hunayn then corrected that Arabic against the Greek, and the last judgment stayed with the reader of the first wording. A corrected leaf went back to the student to be written fair for the patron who had asked for the book.

Working for the sense of a passage, not for a match of word to word, was his way, against the habit of older translators. He read a stretch whole. The meaning stayed with him, and he set it down in clear words, turning a hard term by its use. Clarity came onto the page where a line had once been tied to every foreign word.

His son Ishaq worked beside that labour, and so did his nephew Hubaysh. They took settled passages. Under his eye they carried those passages further into Syriac or into Arabic. The books then moved into the hands of physicians who needed them for their own daily practice.

His first translation was made while he was not yet seventeen, and later it displeased him because the Greek copy had gaps. He had followed the gaps. Years on, he filled the missing places from better manuscripts and made a sound text for a son to copy. The early work was outgrown, and the fuller text was the one that went forward into other hands.

A long search also stands in what he wrote, for one Greek medical book, through Mesopotamia, Syria, Palestine, and Egypt as far as Alexandria. The find was small. He found only about half of it, in Damascus, and that half was enough to begin from though not enough to finish. The half he had could be read and copied, while the rest of the book stayed somewhere still unfound.

Nafi has been listening while his own work waits, and now he shifts the open volume a finger's width closer to the new pen. Dawud takes up the reed. He holds it above the page, the first word chosen for its sense and not for a twin in the source. The word goes down into the line that has been waiting since the pen was cut.

The early versions Hunayn made were written in his own hand. Copyists came later. Two of them, al-Ahwal and al-Azraq, wrote a large angular script called Kufic, with widely spaced lines, on thick paper of great size. Many of those copies were still known centuries on, and such a leaf asks for a wider table than this one.

Galen's medical books stood at the centre of that life's work, and Hunayn translated or revised a great many of them. Physicians wanted the books. Patrons paid for the labour, whether a court in an earlier reign or a doctor who needed a title for his own use. A single work might pass from Greek into Syriac and then into Arabic, each time for a reader with a different need.

Our page is humbler than those broad leaves, and the hand at work is not Hunayn's. Dawud finishes a short passage. Cloth rustles when he shifts his weight on the cushion. Ibrahim offers no talk, and the only speech is the low reading of the model and a brief word of correction at the side.

The professional copyist is used to long sittings, and his posture shows it in the rounded shoulders and the tucked feet. He rolls one ankle. The joint gives a soft click within the leather shoe. Then he settles, and the reed meets the sheet at the same angle he has kept since the first line of this gathering.

This model came with Harith's request, neither a shop rental nor a book Nafi keeps for himself. Harith left it in their care. The patron's volume lies open under Nafi's left hand. He turns its leaves only at the outer edge, where fingers do less harm to the writing along the inner fold.

They fall into a rhythm, phrase and answer, the way two people share a path without needing to look up. Nafi murmurs the copy. The words match the voice coming from across the table. When they do not, the murmur breaks, and the margin receives another note while a finger holds the line in the model.

Near the foot of the page he stops of his own accord and reads the whole side once more with his own eyes. The reed rests across his fingers. He finds one more slip, a plural where the model has the singular. He prepares the outer note for that word rather than trusting the first pass to stand untested.

He sets the mark in the line where the missed word belongs, between the plural and the word after it. Ibrahim leans to see. Nafi lifts his hand away so the note can dry at the edge. The brown sheet lies flat under his palm, and the small writing at the side waits there until the ink is firm.

1:18:58Cakes of Ink: How Ink Was Made · 1,808 words

Past the middle hours we sit in the hired workroom with Dawud the translator and Nafi the copyist, and a dry round of black waits for the next sitting. Dawud sets a smooth stone beside it and breaks a corner free with his thumb. While he grinds, a little water darkens the powder as the pestle turns in slow circles. The black gathers into a paste he can thin whenever the well beside the reed needs filling again.

Nafi slides the older book toward the far edge so the wet paste cannot touch a finished line. The surface shines, and loose grains stay on the board rather than near the margin. He keeps his sleeve clear of the stone while the pestle works. A spare cup of water stands within reach, and he tips a few drops once the paste grows too thick for the reed.

The know-how around this cake belongs to writers who come after our night, and to guides copied in a later century. Treatises of that later age name what a careful hand already did by feel, and their steps let us watch the same motions on this stone. The physician who gathered many recipes had not yet been born. On this shelf a working store of black already waits for the hand that will use it.

His name is al-Razi, and he lives from eight hundred and sixty-five to nine hundred and twenty-five, a full generation after the men at this table. One copy survives. He was a physician as well as a writer on tools, and in that copy he sets out a short treatise on the scribe's craft, with seven recipes for common use. That single late copy is how the list of recipes reaches us.

Gallnut, green vitriol and gum arabic stand as the usual ingredients in his seven recipes, the three a scribe would already know by hand. The mix varies from pot to pot. He writes the list for common use in a workshop, and the treatise keeps to gall, iron salt and gum. A scribe could gather those three in a town market and keep the recipes for ordinary workshop needs.

One ink is for use at once, mixed and taken to the reed the same hour, and the reed takes it. Another is made for storing, or for a traveller who must carry a supply between towns. A stopper and a spare jar sit by the stone for that second kind. The difference lies in how long the black is meant to keep its strength on the road or on the table.

Ibn al-Nadim, writing the Fihrist long after, says that whoever visited al-Razi found him at work, and he was copying. The bookseller records a rough draft or a clean copy, a page always under the physician's hand. The same posture belongs to this table. A man stays bent over a draft while another waits to take the fair copy.

Soot for the black could be burnt from chickpeas, pine cones, pomegranate rind, date stones or charred gallnuts, and each fuel differs. An eleventh-century guide sets those fuels down, and it takes much of its matter from al-Razi, so the choices reach back toward his own notes. The writer chooses by what a kitchen can spare that week. Each fuel leaves its own soot for the stone.

On our stone the powder from a broken disc is already finer than the corner Dawud first broke free. He pauses while Nafi watches the specks vanish and keeps his place at the margin. A few grains still catch the light as pale specks, so Dawud bears down and works them in. The guides want soot ground fine on a stone before it meets the gum.

One later recipe kneads the ash of burnt pomegranate rind with fresh milk and a little gum, and the ash is soft. It is shaped into discs and set to dry, and the milk binds the powder so the round will hold together when a hand lifts it from the board. The round on our table has that same shape. Dawud trusts his own mix for the disc under his hand.

The discs in that recipe dry in the shade, out of a hard sun that would crack them, and a shelf away from the open side of the room does the same office here. Shade keeps the edge firm. A finished round holds its shape if no cup leans on it while the milk is still damp. Nafi moves the water cup a palm's width off, so the damp edge stays clean.

Date stones have their own way in that same later guide, kept as an ordinary kitchen task, and the jar is sealed. Ripe stones go inside, clay is pressed over the mouth, and the jar stays in a hot oven for a day and a night until the stones are like ash. After that they are ground. The black from the ash can be worked up like any other soot.

Another cake is ground with fresh milk for three days, wetted again each time it dries, and then pressed into thin sheets. Three days is slow work. The wetting brings the gum back to life, and the pressing gives a flat piece a traveller could slip between boards. The milk and the waiting both belong to the recipe, so the sheet can travel without crumbling on the road.

Ink recipes were guarded, and each calligrapher kept a mixture of his own, for the know-how was prized. A later tradition remembers that secrecy as part of the craft, and the man at our table keeps his proportions in his hands. What he adds from the cup stays his choice. Under the pestle the paste darkens and thickens as this sitting draws near.

Scribes and booksellers worked under a line of the Qur'an, for Sura sixty-eight opens, Nun, by the pen and what they write, and the words are old. A reed on its rest, a page taking script, and a shop that sells both all sit inside that oath. The labour on this table belongs under the same words. A pen moves, and a line is set down on the sheet.

Our paste is ordinary black, meant to stay, though one writing in his treatise shows itself only at night and another fades away by degrees. Nafi tests a stroke on a scrap so he can see that the black will hold for the fair copy. He tries the reed once and lifts it clear. The fair copy can begin again once that trial stroke has dried to a dull line on the scrap.

A later guide mentions dyed sheets, and later North African leaves turn red, purple and pale pink, while the leaf here keeps the stiff polished brown a ninth-century page is known for. Ours is brown and stiff. He turns the working sheet so the trial scrap stays clear of it, and Nafi's palm holds the lower corner flat. Along its edge the polished face takes the light.

In Fustat, a city of Egypt, used sheets from the eleventh century were kept so the fibre could be pulped again, and pulp can return. Paper was cheap, but not cheap enough to throw away, and a spoiled leaf could go back into another mould. On a low ledge here, a few flawed sheets wait. A later hand could soak and beat them into pulp.

When a long decree was needed, it was made by pasting sheet to sheet, end to end, until the strip was long enough for the text, and the joins overlap. A writer could carry a proclamation that no single mould could have formed, and the paste at each join had to stay thin. A thin join lets the strip roll. No hard ridge catches the hand that holds the strip.

In the sheet we can see faint parallel lines, called laid lines, where the cross-ties of the mould lay under the wet fibre, and they run even. A papermaker's mould leaves that quiet pattern in every leaf he lifts free, and tilted, the lines show as a pale ribbing across the brown. Nafi tilts a corner once. Then he lets the leaf lie flat again under his palm.

Islamic paper carries no watermark, so a sheet is hard to date from any hidden mark in the fibre, and age is read from the script and the record. He reads the hand and smooths the leaf with a fingertip along the ribbing. He leaves the date to the writing itself rather than to a sign in the mould. The brown face shows only those laid lines and the polish of the sheet.

For a long time the Qur'an was still copied on parchment, even while other books took the newer leaf, and parchment is strong. It needs a whole animal skin, and a great deal of work goes into cleaning, stretching and scraping that skin. Only then can a sacred copy begin. A Qur'an on skin cost more in labour than a book on the moulded leaf.

The paste is thin enough now, and he gathers it toward the middle with a flat stick, where the paste holds. A slow scrape lifts most of it into the well beside the reed, and what remains on the stone he leaves to stiffen into the start of another round. Nafi lays the trial reed on its rest, clear of the fresh black. The next line can wait its turn on the sheet.

From the stiffened remainder he pinches a disc no wider than a coin and sets it where the air can finish the drying. The shine fades as the round sits plain, with no mark pressed into it. The surface slowly loses its damp while the air of the room works on it. When it dulls he will move it to the shelf with the other stores, above the reach of a sleeve and safe from the cup.

The shelf holds a jar, a spare reed, and a wrapped lump from an earlier boiling. He reaches up, and his fingers find a clear space between the jar and the wall. He leaves that space empty for the new disc once the air on the table has done its work. The wrapped lump is older and harder, and he leaves it whole while the new round finishes.

He lifts the finished disc from the table, the edge firm and the face dull, and carries it up to the clear space beside the jar. His fingers find the gap and set the dried disc of ink on the shelf, above the stone and clear of the cup. The round stays there after his fingers come away. It is a store for another sitting when this well runs low.

1:31:43A Reader and a Finished Page: A Medical Book in Arabic · 1,319 words

We are with Ibrahim in a courtyard house in Baghdad, on a quiet night in the middle of the ninth century. He sits with a finished copy on a low wooden stand, the reader who has waited for this book. He leans closer. A cool breath crosses the shaded opening and lifts the hem of his sleeve. His thumb keeps the outer edge of the page from curling up as he reads.

The copy is a medical book, written in a fair hand and left to dry through the hours of copying. Ibrahim opens it near the middle, where a fresh section begins. The lines are even. Each letter is dark where the reed was full, and paler where the ink ran thin. The page shows the rhythm of someone who sat long over the copying.

He sets a smooth grey pebble on the left side so the leaf will not lift in the draught. The pebble is still warm from the pocket of his robe. It stays put. His free hand moves along the line without touching the letters. The polished face gives back a soft sheen as he follows the writing.

A linen strip marks the place he means to reach before sleep, and he slides it down a few lines. The strip is frayed. One end is knotted so it cannot slip free of the binding. The knot rests against the inner fold while he reads. Loose threads brush his knuckle as he holds the page open on the stand.

A narrow passage leads from the reading room toward the inner court, where the floor is packed earth swept clean. A clay water jar stands in a small wall niche. The jar is cool. Someone has set a wooden lid on it for the night. A dipper of palm wood hangs from a nail where a hand can find it in the dark.

The inner court holds a small bed of herbs in a clay trough along the wall. Their leaves are damp from a watering earlier in the evening. The scent is faint. A wooden stool stands near the trough, set aside after the day's work. Ibrahim stays with the book, and the stool waits with a folded cloth across its seat.

He rises only long enough to take the dipper from its nail and lift the lid of the jar. Cool water from the jar meets his mouth in a small sip. He drinks slowly. He sets the lid back so nothing falls in, and hangs the dipper on the nail. Then he returns to the stand and finds his place by the knotted strip.

The leaves are gathered in a plain stack and held by a cord along the inner fold. Ibrahim tests the cord with the tip of one finger. It holds. The stack is thick enough to need the wooden stand under it. A spare sheet of brown paper lies beneath the stack, keeping the wood from the lower leaf.

Hunayn ibn Ishaq is the translator most often named for the medical books of this age. If the only Greek manuscript was badly damaged, he might put the work off. The wait could be long. He might fill a gap from a parallel source, or from his knowledge of Galen. Then he could take up the book again and carry the sense forward.

Sometimes Hunayn only revised an earlier translation, and left a serviceable text for the readers who used it. The older work could fail. If it was too poor, he began again from the Greek. The new rendering carried the sense across in a clear hand. The fresh pages then stood in place of the weak rendering he had set aside.

He made Syriac versions for Christian physicians who wanted the Greek medicine in that tongue. Arabic versions went to Muslim doctors, to book collectors, and to other patrons. Ibrahim wants the Arabic. He follows each line for the care of the body. The fair copy on his stand is one more step in that long passing of words.

The leaf he holds belongs to a longer story of paper than this one night's copy. The oldest surviving manuscript on Arab paper is Greek, probably copied in Damascus about the year eight hundred. The date is early. Its letters are Greek, and not the Arabic of this copy. The paper had already reached scribes who wrote in another tongue.

Christians living under Muslim rule used paper as well, and their scribes set Greek letters on sheets like these. Ibrahim keeps to Arabic. A physician in another house might still want the same work in Syriac. His thumb rests near the outer margin, clear of the dark letters on the sheet. He turns no page until the section is finished in his mind.

Another scholar of this age is al-Kindi, called the philosopher of the Arabs, and he worked in Baghdad. He tutored a son of the caliph al-Mu'tasim. The reign was earlier. Al-Mu'tasim ruled from eight hundred and thirty-three to eight hundred and forty-two. Al-Kindi dedicated his book On First Philosophy to that caliph as a work of reasoning.

Scholarly gatherings, called majalis, meet in caliphs' homes or in private houses, and not in the caliph's library. Tonight the room holds Ibrahim and the book alone. One reader remains. He turns a page slowly with the side of his thumb. The sheet makes a small sound against his skin and then lies flat.

Thabit ibn Qurra, a scholar from Harran, may not yet be in Baghdad on this night. He is one who will come, brought by Muhammad of the three brothers. The journey lies ahead. He will work in their circle on mathematics and on astronomy. He will also turn books from one language into another for that household.

He will die in this city in nine hundred and one, after long labour among those brothers' books. That year is far off. The Arabic Elements of Ishaq ibn Hunayn, revised by Thabit, come later than this night. The medical copy on the stand follows an older path. Ibrahim reads it for the care of the body, line by quiet line.

Ibrahim draws the wooden stand a little nearer so the writing sits squarely under his eyes. The letters grow softer toward the far edge of the page. He blinks once. His finger finds the start of the next section without marking the ink. He reads on through a passage about rest and food, the words plain in the new language.

A moth ticks once against the wooden lattice and then moves off into the court. The water jar gives a faint ring as the night air cools the clay. Ibrahim shifts his weight. The cushion under him is worn at the centre from many evenings. A loose thread catches his heel as he settles his weight again.

He reaches the end of the sitting he had promised himself, and lets the last line rest before he moves. The pebble comes off the leaf and goes back beside the stand. The book stays open. With the side of his palm he tests a crease the draught had lifted near the inner margin. He works outward so the ink is not smudged by his hand.

Somewhere in the court a door settles in its frame with a soft wooden sound. The linen strip lies in the gutter where he left it. His eyes stay down. Ibrahim reads the closing line of that section once more. The door stays shut, and the court beyond it gives no further sound.

Ibrahim's hand moves once more across the finished page, slow and flat, from the inner fold toward the clean edge. The paper gives a faint dry sound under his palm. He pauses there. His palm smooths the page a final time, and the crease lies flat where his fingers come to rest.

1:41:25The River before Morning: The Tigris at Dawn · 1,321 words

We come with Layla and Ibrahim to the river bank in Baghdad, in these middle years of the ninth century, as first light spreads thin and pale. The lane is empty. Our steps stay unhurried, and a cool edge meets us that was not in the room above the lane. Mist softens the far bank, and the broad flow keeps a low, even sound.

A round boat rests in the shallows, close against the mud. It sits low. Its frame is built of pomegranate branches, and date-palm fronds are woven all round that frame until the sides make a circle. A coat of natural pitch covers the weave, dark and thick, and one paddle lies across the rim where a hand would find it.

On this bank people call the round boat a guffa, and the name is old. Herodotus already described a boat of this kind on these rivers, many ages before houses rose nearby. The shape has lasted. Its presence in our years is likely, though no writing from these years describes one tied at this bank.

These craft run from one person to a round hull about four or five metres across. The difference is great. Wider figures come from images made long afterward, and they stand only as a range. Builders wanted the most carrying room from the least wood and fibre, and they did not build for speed.

The sides curve outward, and that curve makes the boat very stable. A load sits low. Where the current runs harder toward the middle, a round hull does not roll the way a narrow craft can. Later accounts say that after one long voyage downstream, such a boat was sometimes left behind. The owner kept the paddle rather than haul the empty hull back against the flow.

Other boats share these waters, and they have many names and many shapes. Some are long. They move people and goods from town to town, and in earlier reigns they also carried princes on business and on pleasure. Ropes lie in loose coils on the mud, dark with damp, beside smaller craft, and none of them hurries in this light.

The canal that links the two great streams is the Sarat, and it runs softly. It brings Euphrates water across toward the Tigris, one channel in a wide net of waterways cut through the plain. A side ditch meets our path with a thinner trickle, slipping along to join the broader flow. Dark mud lines that ditch, cool and smooth, with a few reeds leaning over it.

A writer of a following century records advice once given for choosing this site. The counsel is practical. Goods from China come up from the sea, Byzantine wares come down from Mosul, and western boats arrive by the canal. The record is a report of reasons, set down long afterward, and not words spoken beside us on this bank.

We stop for a while where the round hull nudges the mud. The upper pitch is dry. Lower down it stays tacky and dark, where the water has kept it soft through the long hours. A hand rests there a moment, and the woven fronds show through in thin places, while the pomegranate wood feels hard under the dark coat.

A light wind moves over the open water and lifts a few dry fronds on the bank. They tick softly. The sound is small and comes and goes with the wind, never rising into anything sharp. Farther out, ripples travel toward us and fade, and the air smells of wet earth and of resin from the hull.

Layla stands a little apart, her shawl drawn close, watching the slow traffic of the current. She does not speak. A bird crosses low, a dark flick against the pale sky, and is gone over the far side before we can name it. Her hands stay folded in the cloth, and the hem brushes the damp ground when she shifts her weight.

Ibrahim is with us, his arms empty now that the reading is done. He looks tired. He watches the hull rock a finger's width and settle, then rock again, as if the water were breathing against it. His sandals leave a shallow print in the mud, and he stays until the light is fuller.

The sky grows brighter by slow degrees above the open water. Colour comes slowly. Grey gives way to a faint warm tint along the high edge, and the far bank loses some of its blur. A pale band widens above the low mist and touches the tops of the leaning reeds, while we keep our faces toward that change.

Somewhere a wheel creaks on a distant lane, one short sound, and then it stops. Houses are stirring. We hear that stir only as the single creak and as a faint call, too far off to catch any words. A dog answers once from a courtyard and falls quiet, and the water covers those small beginnings so the creak does not return.

The paddle on the rim is worn smooth where many hands have used it. The wood is pale. A cord is tied near the grip, knotted twice, so the shaft cannot slip into the water. Grain shows along the handle, the blade end is darker from long work, and the cord stays stiff with damp when the wind moves.

Mist thins as the light strengthens, and the far side of the water grows a clearer line. We can see low bushes there. They look almost black still, huddled at the edge, their tops just catching the new brightness. A narrow path of ripple runs between us and those bushes, bright for a moment and then dull, while no bird rises from among them.

Our breathing slows to match the water, which was perhaps always this slow. The cool has not left. Light on the shallows is warmer than at our first steps, and a faint warmth touches our hands before it slips away. Wet grit clings to the edge of a sandal and dries pale as the air moves over it.

Layla shifts her shawl higher and looks once toward the houses, then back to the hull. She smiles a little. One hand gathers the cloth at her throat against the cool air, and the smile fades into a quiet face. She stays turned toward the water, the hem of her shawl resting on the damp ground beside her foot.

Ibrahim lowers himself onto a dry rise, knees drawn up and hands loose upon them. The mud is firm there. He watches a bit of leaf turn in an eddy and come back to the same place, again and again. The leaf is brown and curled, and it shines when it tilts toward the light, while his eyes follow that small circle.

A fish breaks the surface once, with a soft pop, and the rings die before the mud. Then it is still. The boat answers with the smallest shift, pitched side meeting the water, then settling. We hear that touch more than we see it, a low pat against the dark coating, while the current keeps its slow pull.

We stand without talking while a thin veil of mist lingers in the lowest places. Time moves softly. Light keeps climbing by degrees we hardly notice, and the far bushes take on a browner edge. Layla and Ibrahim stay near, two quiet figures, their faces turned the same way as ours toward the moving water.

The round boat rocks once more, barely, and then finds its balance against the mud. We stay with it. The paddle does not shift and the dry fronds lie still, while the coating looks darker where the water has wet it. River water laps against the pitched side of the round boat in a small repeated sound, and our eyes grow heavy as we follow it.

1:51:02Goodnight · 227 words

Tonight, we've been a long way. We began in a hired workroom on the west bank, lamp low over brown paper. We stayed with ink and with a Greek book turned into Arabic. The caliph's library stayed a name, a store of books. We passed the round city and its gates, then the stationers' street, shops shut for the night. We sat again over a copy, line by line. A lane, the river's sound, a room at rest. The night was careful work, and then quiet.

Now, it's time to rest. The lamp burns lower. Oil shines in the clay dish. The reed pen lies where it was set down. Paper rests in a small stack, brown in the dim light. A shutter holds the night out. Beyond it, the river moves with a soft, even sound. The street does not stir. Breath grows slow. The room keeps its warmth. The hour needs nothing more.

You don't need to do anything now. Nothing to remember. Nothing to finish. You can let the day go, like the river, moving softly and keeping the same sound. The clay lamp grows small. A pen lies on the wood. Paper rests, brown and quiet. The shutter is shut. Water sounds, far off, even and soft. The room does not stir. All of it holds still.

Goodnight. Until next time, sleep well.
